Now your team does it for a city you haven't modeled: **Chicago**. The Cook County Assessor's Office has to value every home in the county, including the vast majority that didn't sell this year. Assessments drive property tax bills. When they're wrong in a systematic way, some households pay more than their share. A 2017 *Chicago Tribune* investigation, "The Tax Divide," found exactly that in Cook County: lower-value homes were assessed at higher shares of their worth than expensive ones. Build a model that predicts **single-family sale prices in Chicago, 2023–2025**, using only the tools from this course. The file contains **only features of the house itself**. Everything about location is yours to build. ### A real test +---------------------+-----------------------------------------------------+ | File | What's in it | +=====================+=====================================================+ | `chicago_train.csv` | About 80% of the houses, **with** sale prices | +---------------------+-----------------------------------------------------+ | `chicago_test.csv` | The other 20%, **without** sale prices. You predict | | | them; we score you. | +---------------------+-----------------------------------------------------+ The test houses were held out by house, not by sale, so a house that sold twice is entirely on one side. Your CV RMSE is your estimate. Your test RMSE is the truth. **If they're far apart, something leaked.** **Due:** Friday, October 30. All teammates renders the file on their portfolio and every member submits that link on Canvas. One teammate uploads `team_XX_predictions.csv`. **Individual accountability:** Q7 on October 30 asks each of you about *this* model: which features you used and why, your CV and test RMSE, and where the model fails worst. You must predict every test house, so fill NAs in a feature rather than filtering. ## 2. Stay inside the time window Open data from 2023–2025 only. ## 3. No leakage Nothing built from sale prices. *Would the Assessor have this number for a house that didn't sell?* ## 4. The outcome stays in dollars Transform predictors, not `sale_price`. ## 5. Each row has a note saying why you tried | | | it. | +-----------------+--------------------------------------------------------+ | **Features** | Incorporate the feature engineering tricks - including | | | the spatial ones covered these past few weeks. | +-----------------+--------------------------------------------------------+ | **Diagnostics** | Residual maps for your baseline and final model, and | | | what changed. | +-----------------+--------------------------------------------------------+ | **Error | Where your final model fails worst, and whose homes it | | analysis** | over-values (Part 4). | +-----------------+--------------------------------------------------------+ | **Reasoning** | Choices justified by evidence from your own analysis. | +-----------------+--------------------------------------------------------+ ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Part 0: Setup (provided) These helpers are to help you get off the ground. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(tidycensus) library(sf) library(caret) library(spdep) library(nngeo) library(stats) library(dplyr) options(scipen = 999) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} check_na <- function(formula, df) { vars <- all.vars(formula) bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))] if (length(bad) > 0) { stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "), ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).") } } # 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) { df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data check_na(formula, df) set.seed(5080) fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)) fit$results$RMSE } # Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out cv_pred <- function(formula, data) { df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data check_na(formula, df) set.seed(5080) fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10, savePredictions = "final")) fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred) } # Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter. socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) { where <- str_squish(where) q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit) if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE)) url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q) tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson") resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e) if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url) st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE) } # helper function for calculating moran's I # takes in all_sales and list of predictors, uses k=8 for queen weight # example on how to call it: moran_i_cv(all_sales, predictors2) library(sf) library(spdep) moran_i_cv <- function(all_sales, predictors, k = 8) { train <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "train") formula <- reformulate( termlabels = predictors, response = "sale_price" ) cv_predictions <- cv_pred(formula, train) cv_residuals <- train$sale_price - cv_predictions # Extract coordinates safely whether 'train' is an sf object or standard data frame if (inherits(train, "sf")) { coords <- st_coordinates(train) } else if (all(c("lon", "lat") %in% colnames(train))) { coords <- as.matrix(train[, c("lon", "lat")]) } else { stop("`all_sales` must be an 'sf' object or contain 'lon' and 'lat' columns.") } neighbors <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = k)) weights <- nb2listw( neighbors, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE ) result <- moran.test( cv_residuals, weights, zero.policy = TRUE ) # Return the Moran's I statistic numeric value return(unname(result$estimate["Moran I statistic"])) } ``` ::: ### 0a.
